name: Black Green
lede: Black Green is a very dark green-grey that looks nearly black, the name of one of the factory paint colours in the German RAL system.

sections.title: A name from a paint chart
sections.body: The swatch is #31403D, a dark teal-leaning grey with lightness 26 and almost no chroma [1]. Our library traces the name to RAL, the German colour standard first issued in 1927, where it is RAL 6012, and it appears in no other source we hold [1]. The screen value is an approximation of a painted chip [1]. The nearest named colour is [[gunmetal]], at a ΔE of 7.1, and the family it sits in is dark neutrals, between [[black]] and [[dark-green]] [1].

sections.title: What the books say about black and green
sections.body:
The color books do not describe this colour. Every hit in our concordance is the two words side by side in a list [2][3]. Still, the pair is useful for seeing how the words are built. In Pastoureau's account, black and green are two of the six basic colours of Western culture, with white, red, yellow and blue, and heraldry is where the system moved from three basic colours to six [2][3].

Other systems pair them differently. In the Natural Color System, black belongs with white and green with red, as separate opposites [4]. In the Dani language of New Guinea, one of the two colour terms covers black, green, blue and other dark, cool colours, as Kay and Berlin reported [5]. A third, older scheme is Zaccolini's, a seventeenth-century painter's order of colours as distance turns them to atmospheric blue: black, then green, then yellow-green, purple, tan, red, yellow and white [6]. In it, black green is simply the nearest colour of the far end.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 585 paintings, or 2.46 per cent, carry this dark green-black, a colour more common than 76 per cent of the named colours [7]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 3.8 per cent of 1,674 paintings, 2.7 times the rate of the same museums as a whole [7]. In 34 per cent of the 291 paintings that hold it by lightness rank, it plays the shadow [7].

The painter most tied to it is [[painter:paul-cezanne|Cézanne]], with 8 of his 50 works here [7]. In his portrait [[painting:nga-46576|Louis Guillaume]], of 1879, a colour within six units of it covers 57 per cent of the canvas [8]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is a screen colour, not a pigment test [7][8].

The name is 828 years younger than the oldest match, a 1099 Japanese sutra wrapper [7]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a sign of any dye [7]. In Google Books, the phrase *black green* peaks in the 1940s [7].
